summary: Technology Hardware, Storage and Peripherals is splitting in two. Consumer devices are being squeezed by memory costs: IDC data show third-quarter smartphone shipments down 22% and PC shipments down 20% [2][3]. Infrastructure is booming: Dell holds a $95 billion AI server backlog [4], while Seagate and Western Digital earn operating margins near 50% [6][7]. Apple is the large exception, with record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion [1]. Memory pricing is the swing factor for both sides [8]. Sub-industry consensus and current sector multiples were not available to us, so valuation views here rest on single-name data [10][11].

IDC warns the worst is yet to come for smartphones and that weak demand could build inventory into 2027 [3].
IDC says a weaker economy could cut PC demand further into 2027, with channel promotions possible [2].

Whether tariff refunds that flattered Apple and HP margins recur; they are one-off benefits [1][5].

paragraphs: This group is being driven less by the general economic cycle than by an input-cost shock. IDC says memory costs for smartphones have risen about 350% since last year, with sequential increases slowing to the low double digits in the third quarter from roughly 50-100% in earlier quarters [3]. For PCs, IDC says the economy has weakened since last quarter, which could reduce demand further through the rest of 2026 and into 2027 [2]. Pricing will stay well above year-ago levels, and channel concern about inventory could bring promotions in the near term [2]. Consumer-facing hardware therefore faces a squeeze: higher bills of materials meet softer household budgets.

Enterprise-facing hardware sits in a different part of the cycle. Dell's fiscal second quarter 2027 revenue rose 58% to $47.0 billion, with a $95 billion AI server backlog, as data-centre spending ran well ahead of the broader economy [4]. Trade policy is a second macro variable. Apple said tariff refunds added about one percentage point to its September-quarter gross margin and $0.05 to earnings per share [1], and HP's guidance includes $0.19 of tariff-refund benefit for fiscal 2026 [5]. Those are one-off gains, and we would not treat them as run-rate. I did not locate a current source on interest-rate or currency effects specific to this sub-industry, so I make no claim there.

Demand has split in two. Consumer devices are shrinking on price. IDC's preliminary data show third-quarter 2026 smartphone shipments fell 22.0% to 255.3 million units, the largest year-over-year decline IDC has recorded, and it expects growth to stay constrained through 2027 with recovery possibly not until 2028 [3]. Worldwide PC shipments fell 20.1% to 62.7 million units, as early-year pull-forward ahead of price rises and supply constraints removed the usual seasonal lift [2].

Infrastructure demand runs the other way. Dell booked $60.9 billion of AI server orders in one quarter and lifted its fiscal 2027 AI-optimized server revenue outlook to $74 billion from $60 billion [4]. In storage, Western Digital's chief financial officer attributed growth to robust exabyte growth and improved pricing [7], and Seagate guided fiscal second quarter revenue to $4.8 billion, plus or minus $100 million, against $4.2 billion in the quarter just reported [6]. Memory makers are shifting capacity toward AI servers, and TrendForce-sourced reporting says PC DRAM supply could fall in 2027 [8]. Our read is that AI data creation is a structural driver for storage and servers, while for phones and PCs the 2026 decline is mostly a cost-and-price effect that could ease if memory supply loosens. Shortage end-date forecasts vary by company, from 2028 to 2030 for some memory makers [8].

Concentration differs sharply by product. In PCs, IDC's third-quarter data show Lenovo with 23.8% share (14.9 million units), HP 16.5%, Dell 12.1%, Apple 9.5% and ASUS 8.7% [2]. In smartphones, Samsung (22.6%) and Apple (22.4%) lead, followed by Xiaomi (12.0%), OPPO (10.0%) and vivo (7.5%) [3]. Hard drives are described as a virtual duopoly between Seagate and Western Digital in high-capacity drives, though that source gives no share figures [11].

Applying Porter's five forces: supplier power has risen sharply because a handful of memory makers control a scarce input whose cost IDC says is up about 350% for phones [3]. Buyer power is high for PC and phone makers selling to price-sensitive consumers, but weaker for storage vendors, since Western Digital cites deeper customer relationships and expanding visibility into future demand [7]. Threat of substitutes is modest for devices, though cloud storage substitutes for local capacity in some uses. Threat of new entrants is low in hard drives and premium phones, given scale and technology barriers. Rivalry is intense in PCs and Android phones, where Xiaomi, OPPO and vivo saw deeper declines than Samsung and Apple [3]. Pricing power is therefore strongest at Apple, whose September-quarter gross margin was 47.9% [1], and at the storage duopoly, whose gross margins were 57.3% (Seagate, GAAP) [6] and 57.8% (Western Digital, GAAP) [7].

Policy risk is mainly trade. Apple reported tariff refunds that lifted its fiscal fourth quarter gross margin by about one percentage point [1], and HP's guidance includes tariff-refund benefits of $0.08 in its fiscal fourth quarter and $0.19 for the full fiscal 2026 year [5]. Both show tariffs have been a live cost and are now generating one-off reversals. I was unable to open a source on the current tariff status for computers and phones, so I do not characterise the forward tariff regime.

Technology is the other lever. HP said it is mitigating memory costs through pricing, redesigning some PCs and similar actions [5]. In storage, Seagate's chief executive tied its HAMR-based roadmap to meeting growing exabyte demand through areal density gains while maintaining supply discipline [6]. In servers, Dell's traditional servers and networking grew 122% and storage 26% in its latest quarter, showing AI is pulling through adjacent infrastructure [4]. Supply-chain concentration is an emerging risk: suppliers are moving capacity toward AI servers, and one report, unconfirmed by the companies, claims Samsung and SK hynix may cut PC DRAM output by 20% to 40% in 2027 [8]. Treat that as a rumour, not a fact.

Economics are diverging by sub-segment. Apple's September-quarter revenue was $114.5 billion, up 12%, with iPhone at $57.6 billion and Services at a record $31.6 billion; fiscal 2026 revenue was a record $478.8 billion [1]. At Dell, the infrastructure group earned a 15% operating margin against 8.8% a year earlier, while the client group earned $1.14 billion on $15.0 billion of revenue, roughly 7.6% by our arithmetic [4]. HP's Personal Systems margin was 4.6%, down from 5.4%, as higher commodity costs outweighed repricing [5].

Storage vendors are the most profitable. Seagate posted $4.23 billion of revenue, a 57.8% non-GAAP gross margin, a 50.7% non-GAAP operating margin and $1.48 billion of free cash flow in a quarter with only $211 million of capital expenditure [6]. Western Digital reported $4.38 billion of revenue, a 49.1% non-GAAP operating margin and $1.38 billion of free cash flow [7]. Capital intensity is therefore low relative to profit at the drive makers, and operating leverage on price has been large. Super Micro's fiscal fourth quarter adjusted EPS was $1.70 against a $0.92 analyst forecast, although I could not retrieve its margin or revenue from an opened page [12]. I did not find sub-industry ROIC or ROE from a source I opened.

Guidance is strong at the infrastructure and storage end. Dell guided fiscal 2027 revenue to $192 billion, up 69%, and non-GAAP EPS to $25.50, up 148%; for the third quarter it guided revenue to about $49 billion and non-GAAP EPS to $6.50 [4]. Seagate guided fiscal second quarter non-GAAP EPS to $9.20, plus or minus $0.20 [6]; Western Digital guided revenue to $5.1 billion, gross margin to 60%-61% and EPS to $5.80 [7]. HP raised fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $3.19-$3.29 including tariff refunds, and expects PC units to fall in the high teens in the second half [5]. Apple gave no forward guidance in its release [1].

For context on the market, FactSet reports blended third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.2% as of 30 October 2026 and names Information Technology among the sectors with double-digit growth, though it did not give the sector figure in the text I opened [9]. I could not obtain consensus estimates for this sub-industry. Our view is that unit declines of around 20% in phones and PCs [2][3] make consumer-hardware earnings dependent on pricing and mix, so consensus for those names carries more risk than for storage, where guidance already embeds sharply higher pricing. That is judgment, not a sourced estimate.

The most recent sub-industry multiple I could open is dated. Damodaran's January 2026 US dataset for Computers/Peripherals (36 firms) shows a trailing P/E of 81.13, a forward P/E of 36.15 and a PEG ratio of 1.35 [10]. These predate the large price moves since, so I treat them as a historical reference, not a current reading. For the broad market, FactSet put the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 18.7 on 30 October 2026, below the five-year average of 19.8 and the 10-year average of 19.1 [9]. I did not find a current Information Technology sector forward multiple.

Single-name data show wide dispersion. A Motley Fool article lists Seagate at a forward P/E of 25 and Western Digital at 23, with five-year PEG ratios of 0.53 and 0.90 respectively [11]. Those multiples sit on guidance of very high earnings growth, for example Seagate's guided EPS of $9.20 against $7.68 in the prior quarter [6]. Our read is that storage is priced for the memory and exabyte upcycle to persist, and the risk is a normalisation of pricing, while consumer-device names must be judged on whether memory costs can be passed through [2][5]. I did not obtain free-cash-flow yields.

Price momentum is concentrated in storage. A Motley Fool article reports Seagate up 235% year to date and 292% over 12 months, and Western Digital up 164% and 278%; its quote data show both shares falling sharply on 5 November 2026, with Seagate down 16.25% to $466.53 and Western Digital down 17.36% to $267.63 [11]. Whether that reflects earnings reactions or a broader rotation is not stated in the source, and I have not verified the cause.

The fundamental backdrop for those moves is the pricing cycle: DRAM contract prices hit a record in October 2026 while the 128Gb MLC NAND price held flat after 21 months of increases, a pause that may reflect inventory adjustment rather than a turn [8]. Western Digital raised its dividend 17% to $0.175 per share [7], and Seagate repaid about $1.2 billion of debt in the quarter [6], so balance sheets are being repaired while shares trade at high multiples to earnings growth. Apple returned $28 billion in the September quarter [1]. I did not find ETF flow, short-interest or breadth data for this sub-industry from a source I opened, so I do not characterise institutional positioning.
